1.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and controls e4 and d5 without committing a pawn, so Black keeps every set-up open and sees White's plan first. It also makes 2.e4 pointless, since the pawn is simply lost to ...Nxe4. The cost is that Black must be at home in several different structures.

1.Nf3 d5.strategy: Claims the centre at once and turns 2.e4 into a gambit, since ...dxe4 takes the pawn. Black gets an early stake in the middle, but White keeps the choice between quiet set-ups that leave the d5-pawn alone and a direct challenge to it, and Black must be ready for both.

1.Nf3 c5.strategy: Fights for d4 at once: if White takes the centre with a pawn, Black trades a flank pawn for a centre pawn. It suits a player who already answers 1.e4 with 1...c5, but White decides whether the game becomes a Sicilian or a symmetrical English, so Black must be ready for either.

1.Nf3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop and prepares ...d5 while keeping the king's knight and the c-pawn uncommitted. Black can still choose between several solid set-ups. The cost is that White picks the type of game, and after ...d5 the c8-bishop stays hemmed in behind the e6-pawn.

1.Nf3 g6.name: Zukertort Opening: Kingside Fianchetto
1.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 and leaves the centre for later. The fianchettoed bishop presses on White's centre from a distance, and Black counterattacks with pawn breaks in the centre or on the queenside. White can gain space with pawns on e4 and d4, so Black must be ready to hit the centre.

1.Nf3 f5.strategy: Takes control of e4 and aims for set-ups in which Black fights for the centre from the flank. Sound and established, but sharper and more committal than the quieter main replies, because it weakens the e8–h5 diagonal and the e6-square. White can test it at once with the gambit 2.e4 fxe4 3.Ng5, which attacks the e4-pawn.

1.Nf3 c6.name: Zukertort Opening: Slav Invitation
1.Nf3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with the pawn supported, aiming at solid Slav or Caro-Kann structures. It is sound but more passive than the main replies, because the c-pawn move does not develop a piece.

1.Nf3 d6.name: Zukertort Opening: Pirc Invitation
1.Nf3 d6.strategy: Keeps the centre flexible and waits for White to commit. Sound, but it gives White a free hand to build a broad pawn centre, while the d6-pawn only watches e5 and c5.

1.Nf3 b6.name: Zukertort Opening: Queenside Fianchetto Variation
1.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto ...Bb7, which presses on e4 along the long diagonal. The set-up is sound but slow: White can take the centre at once, and Black has to attack the pawns afterwards.

1.Nf3 Nc6.name: Zukertort Opening: Black Mustang Defence
1.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight and watches e5 and d4, so Black keeps its central pawn breaks open. The knight blocks the c-pawn and commits itself before White shows a plan. Sound enough, but Black gains nothing over the main replies.

1.Nf3 a6.name: Zukertort Opening: St. George Defence
1.Nf3 a6.background: 1...a6 is the move of the St. George Defence against 1.e4, on which the English IM Michael Basman did much of the theoretical work and with which Tony Miles beat the reigning world champion Anatoly Karpov at the 1980 European Team Championship in Skara.
1.Nf3 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 and ...Bb7, but spends a tempo on a rim pawn while White takes the centre. Nothing in the position makes the move urgent, so Black falls behind in space and development.

1.Nf3 a5.name: Zukertort Opening: Ware Defence
1.Nf3 a5.strategy: Gains a little space on the queenside but does nothing for the centre or development, and leaves b6 without the a-pawn's protection. White builds a centre and keeps the extra tempo.

1.Nf3 b5.name: Zukertort Opening: Polish Defence
1.Nf3 b5.strategy: Claims queenside space and prepares ...Bb7, but the pawn on b5 needs constant protection and the c6-square is weakened. White gains time against it with e4, which opens the f1-bishop's diagonal to b5, or with a4.

1.Nf3 Na6.strategy: Heads for b4 or c5, but the knight on the rim covers no central square and blocks the a-pawn. White takes space in the centre and keeps the initiative.

1.Nf3 Nh6.strategy: Eyes f5, but the knight on the rim covers no central square, and after 2.d4 the c1-bishop can take it, doubling Black's h-pawns. Black loses time and White gets the centre without a fight.

1.Nf3 f6.name: Zukertort Opening: Arctic Defence
1.Nf3 f6.strategy: Prepares ...e5, but takes the g8-knight's best square and loosens e6 and the e8–h5 diagonal. After 2.e4 e5 3.Nxe5, taking the knight with 3...fxe5? runs into 4.Qh5+ and a decisive attack.

1.Nf3 h6.name: Zukertort Opening: Basman Defence
1.Nf3 h6.strategy: Prepares ...g5 and ...g4 against the knight on f3, but loses a tempo and loosens the kingside. White builds a centre while Black's flank play achieves little.

1.Nf3 h5.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank pawn and gives up control of g5, where White's knight can settle because ...h6 is no longer possible. It does nothing for the centre or development.

1.Nf3 e5.name: Zukertort Opening: Ross Gambit
1.Nf3 e5.strategy: Walks into 2.Nxe5, which wins the unprotected pawn. After 2...Nc6 3.Nxc6 dxc6 Black has open lines and quick development, but not enough for the pawn.

1.Nf3 g5.name: Zukertort Opening: Herrstrom Gambit
1.Nf3 g5.strategy: Offers the g-pawn for nothing: 2.Nxg5 wins it, and 2...e5, which uncovers the queen's attack on the knight, only drives it back while White keeps the extra pawn and Black's kingside stays weakened.

1.Nf3.name: Zukertort Opening
1.Nf3.background: Named after Johannes Zukertort. Most sources call only 1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 the Réti Opening, the line with which Richard Réti beat the reigning world champion Capablanca at New York 1924. Réti championed the hypermodern school of the 1920s, which controlled the centre from a distance rather than occupying it with pawns.

1.Nf3 d6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre at once with the pawn that the f3 knight already supports. Black's ...d6 does not contest d5, so White occupies space without a fight and can build a broad pawn centre that Black must then challenge.

1.Nf3 d6 2.e4.strategy: Occupies the centre with the king's pawn, using the fact that ...d6 gives up the fight for d5. White gains space and open lines for the pieces, but the e4 pawn has no defender yet and must be supported when attacked.

1.Nf3 d6 2.c4.strategy: Gains queenside space and keeps the choice of set-up open, but it does not claim the centre. ...d6 invites White to occupy it, and after this move Black can build a pawn centre of its own at leisure.

1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5.strategy: Takes the pawn that Black has simply offered. The knight stands on an exposed square where it can be harassed, but White only has to be careful with it, and Black's compensation is a quicker development, not anything concrete.

1.Nf3 e5 2.e4.strategy: Declines the pawn and reaches the normal opening in which the e5 pawn is attacked and Black has to defend it. White passes up a free pawn for a familiar game with the usual first-move initiative.

1.Nf3 e5 2.d4.strategy: Hits e5 with a pawn instead of taking it, but lets Black push on with tempo: ...e4 attacks the f3 knight and gains space. White passes up the free pawn for a game in which Black has counterplay.

1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5 Nc6.strategy: Attacks the knight, and if White trades on c6 the recapture doubles the c-pawns but opens the d-file and the c8-bishop's diagonal. Black is still a pawn down, but this is as good as most tries: playable, not more.

1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5 d6.strategy: Kicks the knight at once and opens lines for the c8-bishop and the queen. Black cannot win the pawn back directly, so the plan is a lead in development against a knight that has spent its time grabbing a pawn.

1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5 Qe7.strategy: Attacks the knight with the queen and forces White to move or defend it, but the queen is exposed early and blocks the f8-bishop. White simply keeps the extra pawn, and Black has used a tempo without a lasting gain.

1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5 Nc6 3.Nxc6.strategy: Trades the exposed knight at once and spoils Black's structure: the recapture leaves doubled c-pawns. White stays a pawn up and has a sound game, while Black gets the open d-file and the bishop's diagonal as compensation.

1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3.strategy: Retreats the knight to safety and keeps the extra pawn. Black's knight stands developed on c6, so Black has some lead in development for the pawn, but White has only to finish developing to stay ahead.

1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5 Nc6 3.Nc4.strategy: Keeps the extra pawn for the moment, but ...d5 hits the knight at once and it has to move again, so White loses time while Black takes the centre. Most of White's advantage goes with the tempo.

1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5 Nc6 3.Nxc6 dxc6.name: Zukertort Opening: The Walrus
1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5 Nc6 3.Nxc6 dxc6.strategy: The right recapture: it opens the d-file for the queen and the diagonal for the c8-bishop, the only compensation Black has for the pawn. The doubled pawns are the price, and Black has to play for activity.

1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5 Nc6 3.Nxc6 bxc6.strategy: Recaptures with the b-pawn, which keeps the d-pawn at home and opens the b-file towards b2. The c8-bishop stays shut in behind the d-pawn and there is no open d-file, so the doubled c-pawns come with little activity in return.

1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5 Nc6 3.Nxc6 Qf6.strategy: Ignores the recapture. The knight on c6 simply steps back out of reach, for instance to a5, and Black is left a whole piece and a pawn down.

1.Nf3 f6 2.e4.strategy: Takes the centre at once and punishes the self-block: Black's f-pawn leaves the e8-h5 diagonal loose, so the queen can use it for a check once the knight on f3 moves, and ...e5 is hard to play. White gets space and the easier game.

1.Nf3 f6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn and opens the c1-bishop. Black's ...e5 fails to dxe5 fxe5 Nxe5, a pawn lost, because ...f6 left the e-pawn short of support. Black must settle for a passive set-up while White enjoys space and easy development.

1.Nf3 f6 2.c4.strategy: Takes space on the queenside and controls d5, a flexible set-up that keeps d4 and a fianchetto available. It does not punish the f6 weakness at once, though, and lets Black settle a centre of its own.

1.Nf3 f6 2.e4 Nh6.strategy: Develops the knight to the rim, since the f-pawn took f6 from it. After d4 the c1-bishop eyes the knight, so Black retreats to f7 or accepts doubled pawns after Bxh6. Black is cramped whatever it plays here, and this is no worse than the other tries.

1.Nf3 f6 2.e4 e6.strategy: Controls d5 and frees the f8-bishop, the sound way to build a centre after ...f6. Black is cramped, since the f-pawn takes the natural square from the g8-knight and the e8-h5 diagonal stays weak, but the structure is sound.

1.Nf3 f6 2.e4 d5.strategy: Challenges the e4 pawn at once for a share of the centre. After exd5 the queen recapture runs into Nc3 with a gain of time, so Black spends moves that White spends on development.

1.Nf3 f6 2.e4 Nh6 3.d4.strategy: Takes a second central pawn and opens the queen's bishop against the knight on h6: Bxh6 gxh6 would double Black's pawns. White builds the centre with tempo while Black's knight has to retreat.

1.Nf3 f6 2.e4 Nh6 3.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop to the a2-g8 diagonal, where it controls d5 and e6 and makes the natural ...d5 awkward, since ...Qxd5 would lose the queen to Bxd5. White builds the centre with development rather than pawns.

1.Nf3 f6 2.e4 Nh6 3.d3.strategy: Opens the c1-bishop against the h6 knight, where Bxh6 gxh6 would wreck Black's pawns, and supports the e4 pawn. Modest but flexible; it leaves Black room to hold a share of the centre that the two-square d-pawn advance would take away.

1.Nf3 f6 2.e4 Nh6 3.d4 Nf7.name: Zukertort Opening: Arctic Defence, Drunken Knight Variation
1.Nf3 f6 2.e4 Nh6 3.d4 Nf7.strategy: The principled retreat: the knight leaves h6, where Bxh6 would double the pawns, and guards d6 and e5 in the centre. Black is cramped, since ...f6 cost a move and White has the centre, but the position is sound and free of structural damage.

1.Nf3 f6 2.e4 Nh6 3.d4 e6.strategy: Controls d5 and frees the f8-bishop, but leaves the knight to Bxh6 gxh6. Black gets the two bishops for doubled h-pawns and a weakened kingside, a lasting structural cost.

1.Nf3 f6 2.e4 Nh6 3.d4 d6.strategy: Prepares to meet a central pawn advance and opens the c8-bishop, a solid set-up. It leaves the knight to Bxh6 gxh6, though, which doubles the h-pawns for the bishop pair, so Black develops against a lasting weakness.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4.background: The position belongs to the English Opening and also arises from 1.c4 g6 2.Nf3. The English is named after Howard Staunton, who played 1.c4 in his 1843 match against Saint-Amant and at London 1851, the first international tournament. It did not inspire his contemporaries and caught on only in the twentieth century.
1.Nf3 g6 2.c4.strategy: Claims queenside space and controls d5 without putting a pawn in the centre, so White keeps the choice between a broad centre later and a flexible, strategic set-up. The price is the same freedom for Black, who can build the centre or attack it at leisure. The game is slow and manoeuvring rather than forcing.

1.Nf3 g6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre at once and keeps the c- and e-pawns in reserve to widen it. Black accepts that White has the space and plans to undermine the centre from the flanks and with pieces. The game is a clash between a big centre and the pressure against it, much as in a King's Indian or Modern set-up.

1.Nf3 g6 2.e4.strategy: Occupies the centre and opens the way for the king's bishop, aiming for space and an open game. The e4-pawn has no pawn support yet, so Black can challenge it at once, and the knight on f3 blocks the f-pawn and the queen's diagonal. The game is sharper and more open than after a slow build-up.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3.background: A route into the King's Indian Attack, which Bobby Fischer (mostly in his early career), Mikhail Botvinnik, Vasily Smyslov and Tigran Petrosian all employed. Its use at grandmaster level began as an offshoot of the King's Indian Defence, widespread in the 1950s, with White adopting Black's set-up and an extra move in hand.
1.Nf3 g6 2.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, mirroring Black's set-up. White keeps the centre pawns flexible and puts king safety first, and later decides between slow central play with d3 and e4 and a queenside space grab. The game is strategic and rarely forced early, but Black may take the centre first.

1.Nf3 g6 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2, but 2...Bg7 hits the rook on a1 through the empty b2 square, and 3.Bb2 Bxb2 simply loses a piece, since nothing guards b2. White has to block the diagonal first, so the fianchetto costs an extra move and Black takes the centre in the meantime.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c3.strategy: Prepares d4 with pawn support and blocks the long diagonal in advance of ...Bg7. It develops nothing and takes c3 from the queen's knight, so Black is free to take the centre.

1.Nf3 g6 2.d3.strategy: Supports a later e4 and opens the c1-bishop. It is sound but modest: it claims no space, Black takes the centre first, and White's game stays passive until e4 is pushed.

1.Nf3 g6 2.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop and supports d4. It is solid but passive: the e3-pawn shuts in the c1-bishop, and Black is free to take space in the centre.

1.Nf3 g6 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the second knight and covers e4 and d5. It blocks the c-pawn, so c4 is off for now, and it commits the knight before White has chosen a pawn set-up. The move is sound, but Black can take the centre with ...d5.

1.Nf3 g6 2.a3.strategy: A slow rook-pawn move that prepares b4 but does nothing for the centre or development. Black builds freely while White is still waiting.

1.Nf3 g6 2.a4.strategy: Gains queenside space but weakens b4 and the b3 square and develops nothing. The rook-pawn move is a lost tempo, and Black builds in the centre.

1.Nf3 g6 2.b4.strategy: Grabs queenside space but leaves b2 empty, so 2...Bg7 attacks the rook on a1 at once and White has to block the diagonal. The b4-pawn then becomes a target for ...a5 and ...c5.

1.Nf3 g6 2.h3.strategy: Takes g4 from Black's bishop and knight, but spends a tempo on a rim pawn and does nothing for the centre. Black takes the centre first.

1.Nf3 g6 2.h4.strategy: Prepares h5 against the g6-pawn, but Black can stop it with ...h5 or simply carry on developing. The advance weakens g3 and does nothing for development.

1.Nf3 g6 2.Na3.strategy: Develops the knight to the rim, where it eyes b5 and c4 but blocks the a-pawn and guards nothing in the centre. Black takes the centre with ...d5, which also covers c4, while the knight stays out of play.

1.Nf3 g6 2.Rg1.strategy: Supports a later g4 and g5, but gives up kingside castling and develops nothing. Black takes the centre while White's king stays in the middle for now.

1.Nf3 g6 2.Ng5.strategy: Moves the knight a second time to hit h7 and f7, both of which are defended. After 2...h6 it has to move again, and Black gains time for development.

1.Nf3 g6 2.Nh4.strategy: Moves the knight a second time, to the rim, where it eyes g6, but Nxg6 hxg6 only gives a knight for a pawn. 2...e5 uncovers the queen's attack on h4, and the knight must move again or be defended by a pawn.

1.Nf3 g6 2.Ne5.strategy: Moves the knight a second time to a square where nothing supports it: 2...d6 attacks it and it must move again, so White spends two moves for nothing while Black gains central space and opens the c8-bishop.

1.Nf3 g6 2.Nd4.strategy: Moves the knight a second time to a square where ...e5 or ...c5 attacks it at once. It must move again, and Black gains central space with tempo.

1.Nf3 g6 2.Ng1.strategy: Returns the knight to its starting square and undoes the first move, as if White had passed twice. Black takes the centre while White starts over.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g4.strategy: Weakens the kingside and leaves the pawn undefended, since the knight on f3 blocks the queen's diagonal. After 2...d5 the c8-bishop attacks g4, and White must spend a further move just to keep the pawn.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 Bg7.strategy: Puts the bishop on the long diagonal, where it eyes the centre and the b2 pawn, and keeps every set-up open: a solid pawn centre, a direct strike in the centre, or an early challenge to White's pawns. The cost is that White can take the centre first, and Black must undermine it later.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight with control of e4 and d5 and heads for the same fianchetto structures as ...Bg7. Black keeps the choice between a slower King's Indian set-up and a sharper fight for d5, and White between an early e4 and an early d4.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 c5.strategy: Hits d4 and steers into a symmetrical pawn structure. If White opens the centre and then plays e4, pawns on c4 and e4 restrain ...d5 and ...b5, and Black must rely on piece play. The cost is a restricted game if Black accepts that bind.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 d6.strategy: Covers e5 and c5 and prepares a solid kingside set-up. It is sound but commits early: with the pawn on d6, a later central strike with ...d5 would cost a tempo, and Black has chosen a solid pawn structure over active central play.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 d5.strategy: Strikes at c4 before a piece is developed, and 3.cxd5 makes Black spend moves winning the pawn back. 3...Qxd5 4.Nc3 drives the queen away with a gain of time, and after a developing reply White need not allow the structure Black is after.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 e6.strategy: Covers d5 and f5 and prepares to strike in the centre, with the fianchetto and a knight to follow. It is sound but slow: White can build a broad centre, and the c8-bishop stays shut in behind e6 until the b-pawn moves and frees b7 for it.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 to go with ...Bg7, a double fianchetto that aims both bishops at the centre. It is sound but leaves the centre to White, who can build a broad pawn centre that Black must challenge later.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a solid pawn chain while the bishop and knight are still to come. It is sound but passive: the pawn takes c6 from the b8-knight, and White can later pressure d5 and b7 at once with Qb3.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 f5.strategy: Stakes out e4 and heads for a Dutch-style set-up with the bishop on g7. It is sound but committal: the pawn weakens e6 and the a2-g8 diagonal, and White is not obliged to answer with g3 and Bg2.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight to a natural square where it eyes d4 and e5. It is sound but not recommended: the knight blocks the c-pawn and, after 3.d4 and 4.d5, must move again while White gains space with tempo.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 b5.strategy: Offers the b-pawn so that 3.cxb5 pulls the c-pawn away from the centre. Black can try to open lines on the queenside, but without a pawn on c5 there is no real pawn sacrifice for queenside pressure: the g7-bishop finds b2 guarded by the c1-bishop, and White keeps the extra pawn.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 Na6.strategy: A premature rim move aiming at b4 and c5. The knight guards neither d4 nor e5, so White can take a broad centre while it has still to find a good square.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 Bh6.strategy: Leaves the long diagonal for the c1-h6 diagonal. After 3.d4 the bishops face each other while White holds the centre, and a trade on either square removes the bishop that should guard f6 and h6, the dark squares weakened by ...g6.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 Nh6.strategy: A rim knight that heads for f5, where it is driven back: after 3.d4 Nf5 4.e4 it must move again while White gains the centre with tempo. Black has developed one piece to a poor square and left the centre to White.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 against c4, but spends a tempo on a rim pawn before any piece is developed. White takes the centre at leisure.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 a5.strategy: Restrains b4 but spends a tempo on a rim pawn, weakens b5 and fights neither for the centre nor for development. White gains space unopposed.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the g8-knight, weakens e6 and the a2-g8 diagonal, and develops nothing. White builds a full centre at leisure, and Black's pieces have few good squares.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from White's pieces but spends a tempo on a rim pawn, develops nothing and leaves the g6-pawn without the h-pawn's support. White builds the centre unopposed.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 h5.strategy: Prepares ...h4 but spends a tempo on a rim pawn, weakens g5 and develops nothing. White takes the centre and the h-pawn push gains no time.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 e5.strategy: Hangs the pawn: 3.Nxe5 takes it, and 3...Bg7 is met by 4.d4, which supports the knight, so Black has nothing to show for the lost pawn.

1.Nf3 g6 2.c4 g5.strategy: Loses a pawn at once: nothing defends g5, so 3.Nxg5 wins it, and the knight eyes h7 and f7 while Black has weakened the kingside for nothing.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop on g7 looks down the long diagonal towards d4 and b2, and f8 is cleared for kingside castling. Black mirrors White's set-up and keeps the centre flexible, deciding how to meet White's plan later. The cost is slower central play, since White can take space with c4 and d4 or build a quieter centre with d3 and e4.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square and covers e4 and d5, transposing to the position after 1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6. No pawn has reached the centre yet, so Black keeps every set-up open, and White can still choose between taking space and a quieter build-up.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 c5.strategy: Controls d4 and prepares to develop the b8-knight to c6, with the g7-bishop to add pressure along the long diagonal. If White opens the centre with d4, taking back on d4 leaves White's knight on the diagonal of the g7-bishop; if not, the game can become a symmetrical English-style struggle. Black keeps the central pawn set-up for later.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 d5.strategy: Stakes a claim in the centre and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal towards f5 and g4, reaching the position of 1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6. The d5-pawn has no pawn support and the dark-squared g7-bishop will not guard it, so White can test it with c4 at once, or build the centre more slowly.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 d6.strategy: Frees the c8-bishop and prepares …e5, which the g7-bishop will support, for a set-up with a kingside fianchetto and a knight on f6. It leaves the centre to White for now, so White can develop and build a full centre without hindrance. Sound, but passive.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight, eyes d4 and e5 and supports a later …e5. The knight blocks the c-pawn, though, and White can take space in the centre before Black has chosen a structure. Sound, but …Bg7 first is more flexible.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 c6.strategy: Prepares …d5 with pawn support, after which the c8-bishop can still come out to f5 or g4. The centre is left to White for now, so White can take space at once. Sound, but it commits the c-pawn before the centre is clear.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 e6.strategy: Prepares …d5 and keeps the kingside fianchetto available. Once …d5 is in, the e6-pawn shuts in the c8-bishop, which then needs a queenside fianchetto, while White takes space in the centre. Sound, but passive.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 b6.strategy: Prepares …Bb7 for a double fianchetto with …Bg7: the b7-bishop contests the long light diagonal against White's Bg2, and the g7-bishop covers the dark one. Sound, but no black pawn reaches the centre, so White can build a broad one at leisure.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 f5.strategy: Controls e4 and heads for an aggressive set-up with a fianchettoed bishop and early castling. It loosens e6 and the kingside, and White can simply develop and take the centre. Playable, but double-edged.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 Na6.strategy: Develops the knight to the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but has little influence on the centre. White gains time to develop and take the centre.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5, where e4 would drive the knight away with tempo, and on h6 it does nothing for the centre. White develops and takes the centre at leisure.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 Bh6.strategy: Puts the bishop on h6 instead of g7, where White's c1-bishop meets it as soon as d3 or d4 opens the diagonal. After Bxh6 Nxh6 Black has traded off the dark-squared bishop that should guard f6 and h6, and the knight stands on the rim; avoiding the trade with …Bg7 costs a tempo.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rim-pawn move that at best prepares …b5. White develops, then takes space in the centre.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space and covers b4, but weakens b5 and develops nothing. White develops and takes the centre with a free hand.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 b5.strategy: Gains queenside space and prepares …Bb7, but the b5-pawn stands unprotected, c6 is loosened and nothing is developed. White simply completes development, then a4 or c4 attacks the pawn.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the g8-knight, blocks the long diagonal of the future g7-bishop and loosens e6 and g6, while developing nothing. White develops and takes the centre at leisure.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 h6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a move with nothing yet to prevent and takes the h-pawn's support away from g6. It develops nothing and leaves White free to develop and take the centre.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 h5.strategy: Starts a kingside pawn advance that loosens g5 and g6 and does nothing for the centre or development. White develops, or stops the pawn with h4, and then takes the centre.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 e5.strategy: Leaves the e-pawn unguarded, so 3.Nxe5 wins it. Black can drive the knight away, but White keeps the extra pawn.

1.Nf3 g6 2.g3 g5.strategy: Leaves the g-pawn unguarded, so 3.Nxg5 wins it. …Bh6 drives the knight away, but White keeps the extra pawn.

1.Nf3 Na6 2.e4.strategy: Takes the centre at once against the rim knight. The knight on a6 does not fight for the centre and White can build space, so Black has to prove the knight is useful on the edge by hitting the centre from the flanks.

1.Nf3 Na6 2.d4.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn backed by the knight, while Black's rim knight does nothing about it. A jump to b4 hits c2, but the queen covers it, so White gains space and the choice of how to build on it.

1.Nf3 Na6 2.c4.strategy: Takes the d5 square and queenside space and keeps the choice of central set-up open. White does not claim the centre outright, but Black's knight on the rim does little to stop White building it later.

1.Nf3 Na6 2.e4 c5.strategy: Fights for d4 at once and answers White's centre pawn with a pawn of its own, a flank challenge to the centre. The knight stays awkwardly on the rim, but it can reroute towards c7, where it supports a later central break, and Black's structure stays sound and flexible.

1.Nf3 Na6 2.e4 Nh6.name: Zukertort Opening: Drunken Cavalry Variation
1.Nf3 Na6 2.e4 Nh6.strategy: Puts a second knight on the rim without touching the centre. The h6-knight finds f5 covered by the e-pawn, and the a6-knight stands on the f1-bishop's diagonal, where Bxa6 would double Black's pawns. White builds a broad centre at leisure.

1.Nf3 Na6 2.e4 e6.strategy: Supports ...d5 to challenge e4 and opens the king's bishop, a solid and compact reply. The cost is time: the rim knight still needs a useful square, and White can use the lead in space and development.

1.Nf3 Na6 2.e4 g6.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop to attack the centre from a distance instead of occupying it. Black lets White build a broad centre and counts on piece pressure and a later pawn break; the awkward knight on a6 can find its way to c7.

1.Nf3 Na6 2.e4 d6.strategy: Holds e5 and opens the c8-bishop, a modest move that keeps every set-up open. White keeps the lead in space and the rim knight still needs a useful square, but Black's structure is sound and the pieces can come out freely.

1.Nf3 Nh6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre at once. The knight on h6 sits on the rim, eyeing only f5 and g4 and doing nothing for the centre, so White gains space with no challenge to it and Black must catch up in development.

1.Nf3 Nh6 2.e4.strategy: Claims the centre with the pawn Black's rim knight cannot challenge: the knight on h6 reaches neither e4 nor d5. White gets a broad pawn centre and free development, and Black has to spend time bringing the knight back into play.

1.Nf3 Nh6 2.c4.strategy: Takes space on the queenside and controls d5, so Black cannot easily set up a pawn centre of its own. A flexible, patient choice: White builds up pressure without hurry while the knight on the rim does nothing for Black's development.

1.Nf3 Nh6 2.d4 g6.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto for the king's bishop and gives the rim knight a base, but White can trade a bishop for it at once. Playable and solid, yet passive: White has the central pawn and more space, and Black has to play for counterplay.

1.Nf3 Nh6 2.d4 d5.strategy: Meets the pawn with a pawn and claims a share of the centre at once. If White trades the bishop for the rim knight, Black's pawns are doubled on the h-file, but the bishop pair and the open g-file for the rook are fair compensation, and Black stands solidly in the centre.

1.Nf3 Nh6 2.d4 Nc6.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and pressures d4, giving the position a more natural piece set-up. It is a little loose: White gains space with tempo by pushing the d-pawn, and the bishop can still take the rim knight and double Black's pawns.
